comparedAgainst: https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Rebasing (Pro Git, 'The Perils of Rebasing') — fetched fresh. Pro Git states the golden rule as 'Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on,' and explains the risk in the same terms the article uses (rebase abandons existing commits and creates similar-but-different new ones). Pro Git's own worked example is entirely diagrammatic (labelled boxes C1..C9), never a real terminal session with real hashes, and it never connects the golden rule to git bisect or to a detection technique for merge commits. This article covers the same ground with an actually-run repository (real, verified SHA-1s that visibly differ pre/post-rebase) and goes further into consequences (bisect --first-parent, PR review anchoring, rev-list --min-parents=2 detection) that Pro Git's chapter does not reach.

https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase, git-merge, git-merge-base, git-commit, git-bisect (official reference docs, all fetched fresh) — the article's five inline quotes from these pages (replay/cherry-pick summary, --is-ancestor semantics, the two-parent merge-commit description, plain --fixup's behavior and title format, --first-parent's false-positive rationale, and the NOTES-section rebase warning ending 'the real fix... would be to avoid rebasing the upstream in the first place') were checked word-for-word against the live pages and match exactly, including the exact --autosquash wording ('moved right after the commit they modify').

Atlassian's 'Merging vs. Rebasing' Git tutorial (well-known, long-published, one of the top-ranking pages for this query; its substantive content is client-rendered and could not be re-fetched verbatim in this session, so this comparison relies on the page's well-established, stable structure). It explains the golden rule and shows generic before/after DAG diagrams, but never a real terminal session: no actual commit hashes, no runnable code, no discussion of git bisect or --first-parent, and no technique for telling a rebased history from a merged one after the fact. This article's core angle — one real starting graph, copied once and taken through merge and once through rebase, with the actual resulting SHA-1s compared side by side and shown to differ — is a genuinely more concrete and more verifiable treatment than the abstract-diagram approach most competing pages (including Atlassian's) take.
justification: Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/version-control/rebase-vs-merge.md` from PowerShell three times in a row: PASS, blocks=22, executed=11, every time. Diffing the three `.verify/code/version-control__rebase-vs-merge.json` reports (excluding the checkedAt timestamp) shows they are byte-identical, so every git commit hash the article prints is fully deterministic under the harness's pinned identity (Ada Example / ada@example.com), pinned dates (GIT_AUTHOR_DATE/GIT_COMMITTER_DATE = 2026-01-15T10:00:00+00:00), UTC/C locale and init.defaultBranch=main config — confirmed by reading tools/run-code.mjs directly, not just inferred from the PASS output. I independently replayed the entire bash sequence outside the harness (same pinned env) to cross-check three claims that live in prose rather than inside a `bash run`/`text output` pair and therefore are not covered by run-code.mjs's own pass/fail: `git rev-list --min-parents=2 --count` returns 1 for main, 0 for annotate-for-rebase and 0 for annotate exactly as the 'Choosing merge or rebase' and 'Telling a merged history from a rebased one' sections state; and the reflog for the ref that was rebased really does show 'rebase (start)', repeated 'rebase (pick)' lines (and 'rebase (fixup)' during the --autosquash pass) and 'rebase (finish)', while the ref that was merged shows one single 'merge annotate: Merge made by...' entry, exactly as the closing paragraph claims. Git mechanics are all correct: merge adds one two-parent commit and moves only the checked-out branch, leaving both prior tips reachable and unchanged (verified against the actual merge output, 'ort' strategy, which matches the installed Git 2.52.0 default); rebase checks out the new base and replays each commit as a new object whose hash changes because a commit ID commits to its parent as well as its tree, leaving the old commits dangling except where a second ref (here `annotate`) still names them — I confirmed by hand that the pre- and post-rebase 'reread Dune' commits are different SHA-1s that nonetheless produce an identical diff on the one line that changed, exactly as the article claims. The --fixup/--autosquash demonstration is correct end to end: `--fixup=HEAD~1` targets the right commit, the resulting commit is titled 'fixup! Note: reread Dune' as git-commit's docs specify, and `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash` folds it in (6 commits down to 5) with the fixup line squashed rather than left standing, which I reproduced independently. The golden-rule paragraph and its exercise are technically sound: after a hypothetical force-push, a teammate's old branch tip really would share only 'Add March books' with the new tip (I confirmed this is the correct merge-base for that scenario), and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` really is the right command to detect it, which is the same command the article already demonstrated for the original fast-forward check. The git-bisect --first-parent claim is accurate to the documentation's own reasoning about false positives from broken intermediate commits inside a merged branch, and the rev-list --min-parents=2 --count technique is a real, standard way to count merge commits on a ref (I additionally checked it against `annotate`, which has never been merged into or rebased onto anything, and the article's own exercise correctly anticipates that this gives the same 0 for a different reason than annotate-for-rebase's 0). Both internal cross-links to /version-control/how-git-works/ resolve: I grepped a freshly rebuilt dist/ (via `npx astro build`, not a stale artifact) and found both anchor ids, `git-commit-does-the-same-and-reuses-what-did-not-change` and `a-branch-is-a-41-byte-file-and-a-log-line`, present and correctly generated from those exact headings; the link to /version-control/branching-and-merging/ also resolves (draft: false, present in dist/). The toolchain statement ('The session on this page ran under Git 2.52 in Git Bash on Windows...') sits beside the first real scripted scenario's output block, not in the opening paragraph, matching the pilot-round rule, and 'Git 2.52' matches the machine's actual installed git version (2.52.0.windows.1) exactly. All four exercises are correct: the merge-base --is-ancestor prove-it, the predict-then-verify graph-reading exercise (output correctly hidden inside the solution, not given away under the question), the reasoning-only force-push exercise, and the extend-the-code rev-list check on `annotate` all hold up against an independent run. I found no factual error anywhere in the piece. The only thing keeping this below a clean 9.5+ is a minor robustness point, not a correctness one: two of the article's most specific numeric claims (the rev-list counts in 'Choosing merge or rebase' and the reflog entry shapes in the closing section) are asserted in prose rather than demonstrated in a `bash run`/`text output` pair, so a future silent edit to the scenario could make them wrong without run-code.mjs catching it, even though they are correct today.
